title: Reality Is Faster Than Hierarchy
author: Eddie Killian
summary: Opening on a technician spotting an anomaly at 2:13 a.m., this piece introduces "truth latency": the gap between the moment a condition becomes observable to the person closest to it and the moment someone with the authority to act actually understands its significance. The author argues most organizations measure the wrong half of the problem — response time, repair duration, incident closure — while rarely measuring how long it took the relevant information to climb the org chart before anyone with authority even knew there was an issue. During that latency window, the organization keeps operating on a picture of reality that's already gone stale. The proposed fix isn't eliminating hierarchy or authority, which still matter, but decoupling how information flows from how authority is structured, since organizational rank and proximity to relevant reality are treated as different variables. The piece closes with a concrete diagnostic: take the organization's last major operational surprise, timestamp when it first became observable and when someone with authority understood it, and measure the resulting truth latency.
points: Introduces "truth latency" — the gap between when a condition becomes observable to the person closest to it and when someone with authority to act actually understands its significance.
Most organizations measure response time and repair duration but rarely measure how long it took information to climb the org chart before a decision-maker even knew there was a problem.
The fix isn't eliminating hierarchy or authority, but decoupling information flow from the authority structure — proximity to reality and organizational rank are treated as separate variables.
Offers a concrete diagnostic: take your last major operational surprise, find the timestamp of first observable evidence and the timestamp someone with authority understood it, and measure the gap.
quotes: The hierarchy may not know for hours. The technician tells a lead. The lead decides whether the condition is serious enough to call a supervisor.
Reality moves at the speed of events. Hierarchies move at the speed of information transfer, interpretation, permission, and response.
Far fewer measure the interval between the moment a condition became observable and the moment someone with sufficient authority understood what it meant.
The person closest to a condition may have almost no authority and still possess the most important information in the organization at that moment.

A useful field test begins with the last significant operational surprise your organization experienced. Determine when the first observable evidence appeared. Then determine when someone with sufficient authority to change the outcome understood its significance.
Reality will always move first. The question is how much distance it can accumulate before hierarchy catches up.
